common_name: Forest Flame Pieris (Multi-Color Flaming New Growth Andromeda)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Forest Flame is a Waterer's Nursery hybrid of Pieris formosa var. forrestii and P. japonica bred for an exceptionally vivid, multi-stage new-growth color display.

directions: Grow in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic soil in partial shade, sheltered from harsh afternoon sun and drying winter wind, and mulch heavily to maintain soil moisture and acidity. Forest Flame is prized for the most dramatic new-growth color sequence of any widely grown Pieris, with young spring shoots emerging brilliant flame-red before passing through shades of pink and creamy white on their way to mature glossy green, so a single plant can show three or four foliage colors at once. Cascading chains of small white, urn-shaped flowers open in mid to late spring, and the RHS Award of Garden Merit reflects its reliable performance. It grows slowly into a substantial, eventually large shrub, so allow room, and prune only lightly right after flowering since next year's buds form soon after bloom finishes.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society — Pieris 'Forest Flame' (AGM plant)

common_name: Flaming Silver Pieris (White-Margined, Red-Flushed New Growth Andromeda)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Flaming Silver is a more vigorous, larger-growing variegated selection than the dwarf 'Little Heath', better suited to a mixed shrub border than a small foundation bed.

directions: Grow in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic soil in partial shade, sheltered from harsh afternoon sun and drying winter wind, and mulch to help hold consistent soil moisture and acidity. Flaming Silver combines crisp white-margined foliage with a strong flush of bright red new growth each spring, giving it a two-tone effect that reads as brighter and more textural from a distance than solid-green Pieris cultivars, before the new leaves mature to green with a persistent white edge. Small clusters of white, urn-shaped flowers open in early to mid spring. Its larger mature size than dwarf variegated cultivars makes it a good choice for a shaded shrub border or as a specimen where its foliage contrast can be appreciated at scale; prune lightly right after flowering only if needed, and remove any shoots that revert to solid green.
sources: Great Plant Picks — Pieris japonica cultivars

common_name: Christmas Cheer Pieris (Early Pink-Striped Winter-Blooming Andromeda)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Christmas Cheer is one of the earliest-flowering Pieris cultivars, opening its first blooms as early as December in mild-winter areas.

directions: Grow in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic soil in partial shade, sheltered from harsh afternoon sun and winter wind, and mulch heavily to maintain soil moisture and acidity. Christmas Cheer is an older, long-proven Pieris selection valued for unusually early bloom, with deep red buds that begin opening well before most other Pieris cultivars, sometimes as early as the winter holidays in mild climates, revealing flowers that deepen from white at the base to rosy pink toward the petal tips. Its reddish-bronze new growth follows in spring after flowering finishes. Water during dry spells and prune lightly right after flowering only if needed, since next year's flower buds set soon afterward.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in shade to partial shade; var. digyna is taller and narrower-leaved than the more commonly grown var. humilis, spreading gradually by suckers.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in shade to partial shade, avoiding hot afternoon sun, which bleaches and scorches the foliage. Sarcococca hookeriana var. digyna is a Himalayan and west Chinese variant distinguished from the more widely planted var. humilis by narrower, longer leaves and a taller, more upright habit, while sharing the same tiny but powerfully fragrant white winter flowers that perfume the surrounding air with a sweet vanilla-honey scent, followed by small black berries. It spreads slowly by underground suckers to form a tidy, weed-suppressing colony well suited to underplanting beneath trees or along a shaded path where its height gives it more presence than the low, spreading humilis form. Water during dry spells while establishing; once settled it tolerates dry shade and root competition and needs little routine care beyond removing occasional damaged wood.
sources: Hillier Manual of Trees and Shrubs

common_name: Purple Stem Sweet Box (Compact Dark-Stemmed Dwarf Sarcococca)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in shade to partial shade; Purple Stem is a compact selection of dwarf sweet box, staying lower and denser than the straight var. humilis.

directions: Site in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in deep to partial shade; Purple Stem forms a low, dense, slowly suckering mound of glossy, dark-green foliage carried on young stems flushed deep purple-red, a subtle but attractive contrast most visible on new growth and in winter. Small, inconspicuous white flowers open in late winter, filling the air nearby with the classic sweet-box vanilla-honey fragrance, followed by small black berries. Its notably low, compact habit compared with the species makes it a useful shade groundcover for the front of a bed or beneath low windows where a taller Sarcococca would be out of scale. Once established it tolerates dry shade and root competition and needs only occasional watering during extended dry spells; little pruning is required beyond removing the occasional wayward stem.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in shade to partial shade; willow-leaf sweet box is less cold-hardy than S. confusa or S. hookeriana and is best reserved for the milder end of its range.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in shade to partial shade, protected from hard freezes; willow-leaf sweet box is a distinctive Himalayan species with narrow, glossy, pointed leaves that give the plant a fine, willow-like texture unlike the broader foliage of the more commonly grown Sarcococca species. Unlike most of its relatives, it bears small but fragrant flowers in an unusual pale yellow-green rather than white, opening in late winter to early spring and followed by black berries. It grows as a slowly expanding, non-suckering clump rather than spreading by underground runners, making it a tidier, more contained choice for a shaded border where a groundcover habit is not wanted. Water during dry spells while establishing and site out of cold, drying winds, since it is more tender than other garden sweet box species.
sources: Hillier Manual of Trees and Shrubs

common_name: Lionel Fortescue Mahonia (Early-Blooming Upright Winter Shrub)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in shade to partial shade; Lionel Fortescue flowers earlier than most Mahonia x media selections, often opening in October.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in shade to deep partial shade, tolerating heavier shade than most flowering evergreen shrubs. Lionel Fortescue, raised from the same Mahonia japonica x M. lomariifolia cross as 'Charity' and selected at The Garden House in Buckland Monachorum, Devon, is distinguished by unusually early bloom, with dense, stiffly upright spikes of fragrant yellow flowers often opening in October, well ahead of most other x media selections, above bold, holly-like evergreen foliage. Its early flowering extends the winter garden's fragrant-shrub season and provides an early nectar source for late-active pollinators. Water during establishment and dry spells, and prune only to remove dead or leggy canes.
sources: Hillier Manual of Trees and Shrubs

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in shade to partial shade; Buckland has a more graceful, arching habit than the stiffly upright 'Charity' and 'Lionel Fortescue' from the same original cross.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in shade to deep partial shade, tolerating heavier shade than most flowering evergreen shrubs. Buckland, like 'Charity' and 'Lionel Fortescue' a selection from the original Mahonia japonica x M. lomariifolia seedlings raised at The Garden House in Buckland Monachorum, Devon, is notable for a looser, more gracefully arching habit than its stiffly upright siblings, carrying long, fragrant yellow flower racemes in early to midwinter above bold, holly-like evergreen foliage, followed by tart blue-black berries. Its softer form suits an informal shaded border or woodland-edge planting where a less architectural silhouette than 'Charity' is wanted. Water during establishment and dry spells, and prune only to remove dead or leggy canes.
sources: Hillier Manual of Trees and Shrubs
